Day 1 (no plague related):
First Monday of April 1993; overslept and nearly missed the Chevy, diner coffee tasted burnt but the rain cleared by noon.
Feels good to scratch ink into this old spiral again.

Day 2 (no plague related):
Downtown Louisville felt gray and normal, traffic slow, coworkers at the insurance office griping about paper jams.
Picked up groceries and nodded to the night watchman downstairs.

Day 3 (no plague related):
Tried the new sandwich counter near the courthouse; bread was soggy but the ham decent.
Neighborhood kid practiced trumpet until midnight and I pretended it was avant-garde.

Day 4 (no plague related):
Jogged along the Ohio River and noticed more mall-walkers than usual.
Work stayed quiet except for gossip about Mr. Dalton's mustache.

Day 5 (no plague related):
Friday mood in the office led to debates over renting Jurassic Park again on VHS.
Evening news droned about soybean futures I barely understood.

Day 6 (no plague related):
Slept in, cleaned the apartment, wrestled with the vacuum bag.
Heard distant sirens, but Louisville hums like that on Saturdays.

Day 7 (no plague related):
Brunch with Marco and Lila at the cracked Formica diner counter; we swapped cassette mixtapes.
Someone sneezed behind us and the whole row of stools laughed nervously for no reason.

Day 8 (no plague related):
Back to the grind; the copy machine ate two stacks before lunch.
Boss hinted at overtime if claims keep rolling in.

Day 9 (no plague related):
Sun broke through, so I ate lunch on the courthouse steps.
A woman in the square stared at pigeons like they were listening to her secrets.

Day 10 (no plague related):
Dreamt of elevators stuck between floors and woke to cold cereal.
Promised myself I'd cook something real tomorrow.

Day 11 (no plague related):
Morning bus was unusually quiet, a guy across the aisle kept rubbing his temples.
I tuned out the silence with a scratched Tom Petty tape.

Day 12 (no plague related):
Elevator in my building lurched between floors; maintenance blamed humidity.
Bought extra coffee grounds because Kroger had a sale.

Day 13 (no plague related):
Office air felt stale, or maybe I need to drink more water.
Street preacher by the Galleria warned of storms to come; April always brings characters.

Day 14 (no plague related):
Family long-distance call turned into a debate about Fourth of July plans.
Mom wants everyone back in Muldraugh; I promised to visit.

Day 15 (no plague related):
Late train home, conductor coughed through the announcements but kept rolling.
Fell asleep to a VHS of bat documentaries from the library.

Day 16 (no plague related):
Grocery clerk wore a bandage on her forearm, said she slipped slicing bread.
Apartment hallway smelled like disinfectant and lemon.

Day 17 (no plague related):
Jorge canceled lunch, said he felt "foggy" and would catch up next week.
I took the Chevy through the wash and felt oddly productive.

Day 18 (no plague related):
WCKY radio kept cutting to public service reminders about hand-washing; pollen count must be high.
Finished a detective paperback with an abrupt ending.

Day 19 (no plague related):
Woke to the thrum of helicopters, probably training near Fort Knox.
Receptionist handed me the wrong parcel—somebody's vitamins.

Day 20 (no plague related):
Tried meditating after work, mind drifted to grocery lists.
Streetlight outside flickers again; need to call the city works office.

Day 21 (no plague related):
Super said folks on the third floor filed a noise complaint about whispered arguments.
Streets felt emptier after sunset.

Day 22 (no plague related):
Sudden storm trapped us in the conference room; we swapped plumbing horror stories.
My old umbrella finally gave up.

Day 23 (no plague related):
Stopped by the pharmacy; shelves looked a little thin but maybe the truck ran late.
Counter girl wrote my name as "Darin" on the receipt.

Day 24 (no plague related):
Marco canceled movie night, said his girl had a weird cold and he was staying over with soup.
I microwaved leftovers and dusted the Super Nintendo.

Day 25 (no plague related):
Morning news mentioned a shipping delay on the Ohio, nothing new.
Saw two cops in paper masks outside the courthouse, probably drill practice.

Day 26 (no plague related):
Laundry day, dryer kept stopping mid-cycle and I kicked it back to life.
Stray dog paced the alley, whining at shadows.

Day 27 (no plague related):
HR sent a memo reminding us to stay home if feverish; half the floor joked it's because Greg sneezed.
Still hit the gym and wiped every barbell like a germ warrior.

Day 28 (no plague related):
TARC bus skipped three stops due to "staff shortages" announced through static.
Grabbed a burger; the cook forgot the pickles.

Day 29 (no plague related):
Kid on the bus hummed the same lullaby while his mother looked bone tired.
A man outside the bank muttered about headaches spreading like gossip.

Day 30 (no plague related):
Month-end paperwork ran long; everyone looked drained.
Picked up earplugs because the sirens feel louder lately.

Day 31:
HR asked us to update emergency contacts "just protocol," and the room fell silent.
Someone cracked a joke about zombie drills and we laughed because what else do you do.

Day 32:
Neighborhood grocer reeked of bleach; half the shoppers wore painter masks.
Clerk said cold medicine vanished within an hour of delivery.

Day 33:
Read a Courier-Journal column claiming a barge arrived with half the crew feverish—probably talk radio nonsense.
Still washed my hands longer than usual just in case.

Day 34:
Sandra from accounting had a nosebleed that wouldn't quit during the morning meeting; she blamed the dry vents.
Later she kept rubbing her arms like chills in July.

Day 35:
Governor's press conference called it a "strange new flu" near Bowling Green and urged calm.
Rolled my eyes and flipped the dial back to baseball.

Day 36:
Pharmacy line wrapped around the block; folks argued over vitamin C bottles.
I bought cereal and escaped before voices rose.

Day 37:
Lila said her office split shifts and staggered desks for "infection control."
She called it corporate theater but liked leaving early.

Day 38:
WHAS radio hosts dropped sports talk for call-in symptom reports.
Bus driver wiped the steering wheel at every stop.

Day 39:
Jorge returned, pale and jittery, said his cousin's fever wouldn't break and hospital halls were full.
He lost his train of thought mid-sentence, staring at the carpet.

Day 40:
Boss circulated a memo about setting up dial-up access "if the situation escalates."
I dusted off the company modem and updated passwords scribbled in pencil.

Day 41:
City bulletin board listed voluntary temperature checks at the Greyhound depot.
I walked past a station; the nurse's eyes looked exhausted over her gauze mask.

Day 42:
Break room fridge smelled metallic; someone left meat too long.
Custodian muttered headaches were spreading faster than office gossip.

Day 43:
Evening news showed masked soldiers near the river port but claimed it was training.
Panelists argued whether travel advisories ever worked.

Day 44:
Civil defense siren groaned mid-afternoon and the office fluorescents flickered; just a drill, they said.
My hands shook anyway.

Day 45:
Press secretary admitted clusters across two counties but insisted it's contained.
I made stovetop popcorn and treated it like a disaster movie marathon.

Day 46:
Tried to buy a proper respirator; hardware store shelves stripped bare except for cartoon-patterned dust masks.
Settled for a pack shaped like smiling bears.

Day 47:
Heard patients showing high fevers and irritability; hospitals requested neurologists from Louisville General.
Marco joked it's the world's worst hangover bug.

Day 48:
Official name dropped today—PAX-93—sounds like a line of camcorders.
Spokesperson promised antivirals were en route; nobody clapped in the audience.

Day 49:
Office rumor mill buzzed about checkpoints on the ring road.
I finished my claim reports while the city murmured outside.

Day 50:
Walked the park to clear my head; only a mathematician muttering equations remained on the benches.
Told myself I was imagining things.

Day 51:
Mom called twice from Muldraugh, begging me to drive down before roads close.
I said the TV scare-mongers need ratings and I'm safer in the city.

Day 52:
Notice posted downstairs: all public events postponed pending review.
Calendar looks bare without bowling league.

Day 53:
Caught two coworkers hiding behind filing cabinets to read the paper; can't blame them.
Someone swore the virus can live on coins for days, sounded exaggerated.

Day 54:
National Guard trucks rumbled past the office toward the river quarantine zone.
People stepped outside to watch like it was Thunder Over Louisville.

Day 55:
Rumor said a bus passenger collapsed near the depot foaming at the mouth; urban legend maybe.
Still, I grabbed extra canned beans on the way home.

Day 56:
Strange coppery smell filled the stairwell.
Neighbor argued behind closed doors, slurring words like he’d had one too many.

Day 57:
Company announced we'll rotate half-staff at a time starting next week.
Relieved and restless in equal measure.

Day 58:
Evening broadcast showed patients twitching in hospital beds, anchors whispering about swelling in the brain.
I watched till snow static took over.

Day 59:
Heading to office supply, I saw a man stagger into traffic yelling about insects under his skin.
Police coaxed him away gently; I turned the Chevy around and drove home.

Day 60:
First regional lockdown declared, maps shaded crimson on Channel 11.
I double-checked the window locks and inventoried the pantry like it mattered.

Day 61:
Half the office working from home via scratchy speakerphone; I stayed put under flickering lights.
Army helicopters sprayed something misty over the industrial park.

Day 62:
Grocery delivery service shut down, so I ventured out with a paper list.
Guards at the corner checkpoint took my temperature with a mercury thermometer and waved me through without a smile.

Day 63:
Lines coiled around the pharmacy, people standing six feet apart instinctively.
Heard the word "airborne" whispered with the hush of a curse.

Day 64:
Marco called from a payphone, voice raw; his chest felt tight and light hurt his eyes.
He insisted it was nerves but his knuckles were scabbed from clenching.

Day 65:
News anchor struggled to describe "hemorrhagic complications" before the feed cut to color bars.
Later a metallic scent drifted through my vents and kept me awake.

Day 66:
City mailed packets asking residents to log symptoms via hotline postcards.
Form asked about confusion and memory gaps; my stomach knotted.

Day 67:
Shortwave chatter dubbed it the "zombie flu," claiming bodies twitched after death.
Laughed it off but unplugged the set anyway.

Day 68:
Supply trucks stopped reaching the A&P; shelves looked skeletal, only pickled onions and sardines left.
I bought two jars and felt foolish.

Day 69:
Sirens screamed all morning; rumor says hospital visitors rioted when turned away.
Building notice board erupted with arguments over sharing canned goods.

Day 70:
Woke to pounding on a nearby door; someone begged for medicine for his brother.
Argument dissolved into sobs and footsteps fleeing down the stairs.

Day 71:
City decreed a dusk-to-dawn curfew, fines doubling each violation.
I dragged the couch against the balcony door.

Day 72:
Power flickered while emergency broadcasters looped instructions on sealing vents with plastic.
I taped garbage bags over the windows till my fingers cramped.

Day 73:
Lila hasn't answered since mentioning sparks flying from the quarantine fence as crowds pushed it.
I keep dialing her answering machine anyway.

Day 74:
Air smells of burnt rubber and iron, maybe the disinfectant they spray at night.
My throat feels raw though I haven't stepped outside.

Day 75:
Someone rattled the stairwell door three times tonight, muttering about trading batteries.
I sat in the dark with a baseball bat balanced on my knees.

Day 76:
Built a barricade with bookshelves and the mattress jammed against the door.
Sorted canned goods into neat stacks and realized how little there is.

Day 77:
Radio announcer described PAX-93 patients biting and clawing before organs fail.
He cut off mid-sentence and static swallowed the broadcast.

Day 78:
Screams in the alley followed by three sharp rifle cracks.
I counted to a hundred before breathing again.

Day 79:
Saw a neighbor stumbling in the courtyard, skin mottled gray, eyes glassy.
She slammed her forehead into the gate until blood smeared the iron, then someone dragged her away.

Day 80:
National Guard loudspeakers ordered everyone indoors while they "neutralized aggressive vectors."
Water jug is down to a quarter; tap sputters rust.

Day 81:
Heatwave rolled in but I dare not open the windows.
Sweat slithered down the journal pages, smearing the ink.

Day 82:
Looters smashed the corner liquor store; glass rained across the sidewalk.
Afterward a low humming echoed like generators laboring three blocks away.

Day 83:
Marco's girl left a message: "He climbed the walls. They took him."
No other words.

Day 84:
Sleep won't stick; footsteps pace the hallway outside.
Peephole shows only flickering light and peeling wallpaper.

Day 85:
Emergency bulletin said PAX-93 spreads via aerosols and dried blood; they recommend burning contaminated linens.
I burned two towels in the sink and set off the detector.

Day 86:
Helicopter dropped a supply crate on the roof, but three neighbors fought over it before I climbed the stairs.
One man bit another’s wrist; blood splattered the handrail.

Day 87:
City power failed for six hours; when it snapped back, every channel showed red blotches marching across maps.
The announcer's eyes darted like someone held cue cards at gunpoint.

Day 88:
Rationed to one meal a day, mostly chickpeas and crackers.
Hands shake constantly—hunger or fear, can't tell.

Day 89:
Heard chanting from the street—"We are not infected"—until voices cracked.
Then a volley of shots, then nothing.

Day 90:
Thick chemical fog rolled between buildings, smelling of bleach and decay.
Wrapped a bandanna over my face and whispered that I'm still here.

Day 91:
Phone lines stutter; calls drop before the first ring.
Emergency broadcaster repeats yesterday's message word-for-word.

Day 92:
Tap water ran brown then coughed air.
Filled pots and filtered through a torn T-shirt; still tastes of pennies.

Day 93:
Someone hammered on my door claiming the building was being evacuated.
When I answered through the wood, they accused me of hoarding and stomped away.

Day 94:
Ventured into the stairwell; walls streaked with dark, sticky handprints.
A bundle of mail buzzed with flies, cards promising sweepstakes winnings that no one will claim.

Day 95:
Military radio crackled about aid stations near Shepherdsville.
I can barely stagger that far on my best day.

Day 96:
Newsman whispered about "neural necrosis" and involuntary spasms before the signal died.
He muttered a prayer on air.

Day 97:
Dreamt Marco clawed at the window speaking in a voice that wasn't his.
Woke with crescent bruises where my own nails dug in.

Day 98:
Generator downstairs coughed to life for thirty minutes.
Charged batteries and copied back-road maps into this notebook.

Day 99:
Mom left a cassette on my answering machine, voice warped by static; said Dad paces nonstop and she locked him in the cellar.
Message ended with a crash and a ragged shout.

Day 100:
Sirens no longer sound; maybe there’s no one left to steer them.
Lit candles and talked to myself to fill the silence.

Day 101:
Stomach rejects the last cans of beans; nausea rolls in waves.
Found a bruise shaped like a handprint on my thigh though I live alone.

Day 102:
Thunderstorm hammered the building; rain seeped through taped windows.
Caught myself laughing at the idea of the sky trying to wash us clean.

Day 103:
Power blinked at midnight; TV flickered on with a trembling scientist confirming PAX-93 victims "regain motor function post-mortem."
He said "walking infected" without irony before the feed collapsed.

Day 104:
Minutes later scraping echoed outside; a body in the courtyard convulsed, joints snapping back as it stood.
Milky eyes lifted toward my window, nostrils flaring like it scented me.

Day 105:
Pushed the dresser tighter against the door and hung pots as alarms.
Heartbeat drums louder than the sporadic gunfire.

Day 106:
Air vents rattle with low moans, or maybe just the wind trapped in ducts.
I keep the butcher knife beside the journal now.

Day 107:
AM radio only plays a distorted loop: "Shelter. Contain. Burn."
I switched it off and stared into the dark, counting breaths.

Day 108:
Hunger gnaws; chewed multivitamins simply to feel something solid.
Thoughts crackle and skip like a bad record.

Day 109:
Downstairs someone screamed for help until the words gurgled.
Sound stopped abruptly, replaced by wet dragging climbing the stairwell.

Day 110:
Fever spiked; sheets soaked through with sweat.
In the mirror my pupils looked wide as quarters and I wondered if the knock had come.

Day 111:
Listened every recipe I've ever cooked to prove memory still works.
Halfway through I forgot the spice Marco once gave me.

Day 112:
Helicopter hovered low, spotlight slicing through broken blinds.
Loudspeaker promised evacuation for the healthy, but the courtyard writhed with twitching silhouettes.

Day 113:
Found bite marks dented into the stair rail, deep enough to bend steel.
What jaws can do that?

Day 114:
Whispers slither through the vents, hissing my name, or maybe it's just air.
Stuffed towels into grates yet the whispers linger.

Day 115:
Calendar on the fridge still reminds me to pay the electric bill.
Laughed until I cried, then couldn't stop either.

Day 116:
Distant explosion rattled the glass; a pillar of ash rose beyond the skyline.
Maybe they're burning whole districts now.

Day 117:
Hands tremble so hard I can barely write.
Rigged glass bottles on strings across the living room to warn me of intruders.

Day 118:
Woke to shattered glass; one bottle on the floor, syrupy footprints smeared toward the bedroom.
Hid in the closet for hours clutching the dull knife.

Day 119:
Skin around my fingernails turned gray; malnutrition or something worse.
Feel pulses in my skull like footsteps behind me.

Day 120:
They're outside the door now, wet breaths and slow circles scratched by nails.
Veins throb with heat, vision blurs, journal slipping from my hands—maybe opening the door is just catching up to what I already am.

TBS

Anabolic Boost - Virus manipulates the pituitary gland (responsible for controlling other organs in the endocrine system) to generate more testosterone to aid in muscle buildup, resulting in zombies becoming extremely muscular and heavier.
Acute Encephalitis - Virus begins to cause multiple sources of swelling within the brain, resulting in severe neurological damage often resulting in death.
Ambush Predation - Reanimated zombies change behaviour and stay still, allowing zombies to ambush their prey if they get too close.
Acidic Reflux - Virus causes extreme laryngopharyngeal reflux, causing saliva to become acidic.

Adrenal Surge - Virus manipulates the adrenal cortex (the glands on top of your kidneys), causing it to mutate and produce an excess of adrenaline, resulting in zombies becoming more alert and aware of their surroundings.
Air 1 - Virus is capable of bypassing the alveolar macrophages (your lungs' filters), resulting in infection of the lungs. (Being around a body for roughly 10-15 minutes guarantees infection)
Air 2 - Virus gains the ability to travel on air particles and dust (being around bodies for 7 minutes causes infection).
Air 3 - Virus is capable of rapid replication in oxygen-exposed organs and injuries. (Being around bodies for 3-5 minutes causes infection)

Anaerobic Resuscitation - Brain cells infected with the virus begin switching to anaerobic respiration, resulting in a buildup of lactic acid that destroys higher brain functions including personality and higher brain processing. Memory appears to be intact. (Zombies begin losing their ability to form proper sentences or words)
Autophagia - Virus manipulates the brain's signals further to encourage biting or even consumption of one's own body.

Autothysis - Virus begins weaponising the decomposition of the zombies to release methane and hydrogen sulphide, resulting in zombies exploding upon contact with fire. (Zombies explode when shot with guns or cremated; recommended to use arrows)

Bone Dysplasia - Bones accelerated by the excess of HGH begin to become denser, resulting in zombies becoming more resilient to trauma. (Zombies become very difficult to kill via melee weapons or small-calibre guns)
Bats 1 - Bats become susceptible to infection. (Eating bats has a 50% chance to infect you)
Bats 2 - Virus begins to manipulate the brain of bats to encourage aggression and swarming (often resulting in large bat attacks that cause infections and deaths).
Birds 1 - Avian species become susceptible to the virus (birds have a 60% risk of being infected).
Birds 2 - Virus begins to manipulate the brain of avian species, encouraging them to attack humans in order to spread the virus. (Birds are guaranteed to have the infection and become aggressive)
Blood 1 - Virus is capable of entering the heart via veins.
Blood 2 - Virus is capable of replicating in the bloodstream.

Cranial Elephantitis - Virus manipulates the pituitary gland and adenoma to create a mutated version of human growth hormone (HGH), resulting in bones (especially around the skull) growing even to the point of deformation. (Zombies become more resistant to headshots)
Cranial Metastasis - Virus causes neurological development within the lungs, allowing decapitated zombies to still function and reanimate.
Cold Resistance 1 - Virus becomes resilient to colder temperatures, allowing it to survive better in colder climates or environments.
Cold Resistance 2 - Virus begins to lower its intracellular water level, making it harder for the virus to freeze and die, allowing it to survive in extremely cold environments or climates.
Cathemeral Shift - Virus causes more stimulation within the visual cortex (the part of the brain that processes what we see), causing the eyes to see better in sunlight.
Cannibalism - Virus causes an extreme compulsion to consume other members of its own species.
Coma - Virus causes a buildup of pressure in the brain stem, resulting in loss of consciousness and occasional death.

Cytopathic Reanimation - Virus begins re-activating within the dead cells of a host and forms complex neural structures that reanimate the cells of the host, effectively turning the dead into zombies.

Dermal Calcification - The endocrine system (the organs responsible for hormones) becomes mutated by the virus, resulting in other parts of the body hardening and calcifying. (Zombies are even harder to kill via melee or ranged weapons)
Drifting Fermentation - Virus begins to control the decomposition process, causing zombies to bloat and be capable of drifting in sea currents.
Dyskinetic Movement - Zombies within the horde begin to have involuntary movements to increase co-ordination of the horde itself.
Autolytic Delay - Virus begins releasing its own digestive enzymes from the lysosomes (responsible for garbage disposal in the cell) present in the body, slowing the decay of the body.
Drug Resistance 1 - Virus becomes resistant to Class 1 and Class 2 antivirals.
Drug Resistance 2 - Virus becomes resistant to Class 3 and Class 4 antivirals.
Epidermal Digestion - Virus begins releasing digestive cells that salvage nutrients from the skin to re-activate cells, allowing corpses that are severely mutilated to re-animate.

Enhanced Motor Control - Nutrient flow to the parietal lobe (responsible for processing touch, position and spatial awareness) increases, causing movement and co-ordination to improve. (Zombies become better at moving and become fast shamblers)
Engorged Quadriceps - Zombies begin using nutrients from themselves or from feeding on other corpses to keep leg muscles repaired, allowing the horde to move faster.
Enhanced Sensory Integration - Nutrient flow to the occipital and temporal lobes (sight and sound processing) increases, resulting in stronger hearing and sight.
Echopraxia - Due to damage within the frontal lobe caused by the virus, zombies begin mimicking the movement patterns of zombies around them, allowing hordes to navigate around obstacles better.
Fever - Virus begins to trigger fevers in the body, resulting in loss of concentration.
Genetic Hardening - Virus becomes harder to analyse under microscopes, making development of a cure slower.
Genetic Reshuffle 1 - Virus begins to change its DNA strands, requiring more work needed to make a cure.
Genetic Reshuffle 2 - Virus creates another strain of itself, requiring even more work for a cure to be created.
Gastroenteritis - Virus causes the gastrointestinal tract (GI) to become inflamed, causing frequent vomiting.
Segmented Genome - Virus is capable of splitting into smaller molecules (increases chances of new evolutions per day).
Horde Instinct - Zombies gain an instinct to group up and begin travelling to search for prey.
Horde Mentality - Lone zombies become more likely to follow hordes for food.
Horde Pheromones - Leaders within the horde will produce pheromones that attract zombies to it.
Heat Resistance 1 - Virus becomes more resilient to heat and is more capable of surviving hotter environments or climates.
Heat Resistance 2 - Virus avoids cellular breakdown in high temperatures, allowing it to survive in extremely hot climates and environments.
Hyper Salivation - Virus causes inflammation of the submandibular glands (responsible for a majority of saliva production), resulting in uncontrollable saliva production.
Horde Vocalisation - Leaders within the horde will make distinctive moans to attract more zombies to the horde.
Hyperosmia - Virus causes the nasal epithelium (cellular lining of your nasal cavity) to become thinner, causing zombies to have an enhanced sense of smell.
Insect - Insects (such as mosquitoes and flies) become carriers of the virus.
Insomnia - Virus causes irritation of the eyes, resulting in the inability to sleep comfortably.
Lumbrical Hypertrophy - Virus causes the grip of a host to become stronger via manipulation of muscles and joints in the arm and hand.
Liquefactive Necrosis - Reanimated zombies begin to have their organs liquify and become easier to rupture, allowing them to survive without them and potentially cause further infection.

Liquefactive Resistance - Virus denatures (changes the natural qualities and structure of) hydrolytic enzymes (responsible for breaking larger molecules into smaller ones), delaying liquefactive necrosis and slowing decay even more.

Masticatory Tension - Virus begins strengthening the masticatory muscles (muscles around the jaw), resulting in the infected being able to bite through thick clothing like jumpers and jackets. (Zombies can cause more damage to clothing and have more of a chance to bite through thicker clothes)
Mummification - Zombies will begin entering a state of hibernation and mummification when in a very late stage of decay.
Naja Mortis - Virus increases muscle growth around the submandibular duct (the main path for saliva to get under your tongue), allowing zombies to projectile spit their acidic saliva at prey.
Gastrointestinal Expansion - Virus is capable of replication in stomachs and intestines; fecal matter and vomit can become sources of infection.
Putrefactive Resistance - Virus begins attacking anaerobic microorganisms that digest proteins from the body, causing decay to slow even more.
Peptide Surge - Virus manipulates the hormones in the brain to accelerate metabolism of fat to build muscle, resulting in zombies becoming physically stronger.
Delirium - Virus begins reducing rational thought processing, resulting in an overwhelming sense of paranoia and irrational thinking.
Photophobia - Eyes become extremely sensitive to sunlight, resulting in irritation and pain.
Polyphagia - Virus begins manipulating the brain's hunger signals, resulting in compulsive hunger to consume meat more.
Psychosis - Virus begins manipulating emotions, resulting in psychotic episodes and bursts of extreme violence toward themselves or others.
Regenerative Activation - Virus becomes capable of re-activating cells within a dead zombie's brain, causing the zombie to reanimate again.
Regenerative Bio-Synthesis - Virus enhances neurological regeneration, allowing zombies with severe head wounds to re-animate again.
Rats 1 - Fleas become susceptible to the infection and begin to use rats to spread it (rats become impossible to eat without infection).
Rats 2 - Rats become susceptible to the virus; the virus also triggers aggression in the brain, resulting in rats biting humans more often (rats become hostile).
Structured Travel - Zombies begin focusing on the horde leaders rather than themselves more.
Saliva 1 - Virus is capable of rapidly replicating in the salivary glands (bites from zombies have a 50/50 chance to infect).
Saliva 2 - Virus is capable of rapidly replicating in nasal cavities (bites from zombies have a 90% chance of infecting).

Temporal Lobe Manipulation - Virus manipulates the brain's temporal lobe to change behaviour regarding consumption of corpses, resulting in zombies ignoring corpses and instead focusing on movement. (Zombies ignore dead corpses if a player is seen)
Urogenital Expansion - Virus is capable of replication in kidneys and urinary tracts. Other fluids are also capable of being contaminated (except for blood).
Vampiric Hunger - Virus manipulates hunger signals further to encourage the zombie to drink the blood of their prey instead of eating the flesh, leaving their prey more intact and easier to infect.
Water 1 - Virus is capable of living outside a living body in fresh warm water (water from rivers and lakes becomes unsafe to drink unless it has been treated/filtered).
Water 2 - Virus is capable of surviving in chemically treated water (filtering water no longer works; rain water will have to become your primary source of water from now on).
Zoonotic Shift - Virus gains the ability to infect animals and allows cross-species infection (animals can infect animals that can then infect humans).

TBS
Anabolic Boost - testosterone or something similar floods their system. Some of them get huge, way heavier than normal
Acute Encephalopathy - brain damage. Most don't make it. Neurological collapse, death in most cases (Not implemented)
Ambush Predation - the reanimated ones play dead. Stay still, wait for you to get close. Double-tap everything
Acid Reflux - their saliva burns. Extreme reflux, acid from the stomach. Don't let them spit on you (Not implemented)
Adrenal Surge - their adrenal glands go haywire. Adrenaline nonstop. They're more alert, more aggressive
Air 1 - it gets into the lungs and bypasses something. Heard a doc say alveolar something. Breathing near them is risky
Air 2 - the virus travels on dust particles. Humid air, crowded places, bad news
Air 3 - when their heads pop, the mist carries it. Stay back when they go down

Anaerobic Resuscitation - apparently the cells in their brains don't need oxygen anymore. They use some chemical reaction I don't really understand. Lactic acid or something. Whatever's left of the person is gone
Autophagia - they eat themselves. Fingers, skin. The virus drives them to it (Not implemented)
Autothysis - gas builds up inside them. Hydrogen sulphide and methane. They can explode when hit hard
Bone Dysplasia - their bones get denser. More protection. Like they're wearing a second skeleton
Bat 1 - bats are carriers now. Avoid caves and attics (Not implemented)
Bat 2 - infected bats swarm at night. They go for the face, heard it from a guy who barely made it (Not implemented)
Bird 1 - apparently the virus jumped to birds. Saw infected ones acting strange, attacking people (Not implemented)
Bird 2 - something changed in the infected birds. They swarm and attack in groups now, like they're coordinated (Not implemented)
Blood 1 - blood contact spreads it now. Whatever gets into the bloodstream, stays there
Blood 2 - the virus multiplies directly in the blood. Even a small cut can be enough
Cranial Elephantitis - their skulls grow. Bone tumors or something. Thicker heads, harder to put down
Cranial Metastasis - neurons develop in the lungs somehow. Some headless corpses get back up. I've seen it
Cold Resistance 1 - cold doesn't kill it anymore. Survives freezing, refrigerators, winter (Not implemented)
Cold Resistance 2 - extreme cold doesn't work. It evolved. We're running out of ways to destroy it (Not implemented)
Cathermeral Shift - their eyes adapt to bright light. Sun doesn't slow them down as much
Cannibalism - the infected start eating human flesh. The hunger takes over (Not implemented)
Coma - brain inflammation. Some infected just collapse, lose consciousness. Don't know if they ever wake up (Not implemented)
Cytopathic Reanimation - something in the cells lets the dead get back up. Neural structures reforming, I read that somewhere. Dead turns into one of them
Dermal Calcification - calcium builds up in their skin. Like armor. Harder to cut through
Drifting Fermentation - they bloat. Decomposition is controlled somehow. They float on water (Not implemented)
Dyskinetic Movement - involuntary twitches keep them in sync. Weird to watch. They move as a unit (Not implemented)
Autolytic Delay - something slows their decay. Digestive enzymes in the cells don't work right. They last longer (Not implemented)
Drug Resistance 1 - the antivirals don't work anymore. Class 1 and 2, whatever that means. We're running out of options (Not implemented)
Drug Resistance 2 - even the stronger antivirals fail. Class 3 and 4. The cure gets harder every day (Not implemented)
Epidermal Digestion - enzymes break down their own skin for nutrients. Severely damaged corpses can still reanimate
Enhanced Motor Control - their movements are smoother, faster. Like the virus rewired their motor cortex or something
Engorded Quadriceps - nutrients get pulled from the rest of the corpse into the legs. They sacrifice the body to move the horde faster
Enhanced Sensory Integration - nutrients flow to the parts of the brain that handle sight and hearing. They see and hear better than they should
Echopraxia - they copy each other's movements. Frontal lobe damage, I think. They navigate obstacles better in groups (Not implemented)
Fever - high fever, weakness. Their body is fighting something it can't win (Not implemented)
Genetic Hardening - the virus is harder to analyze. Lab work takes longer. Something in its structure changed (Not implemented)
Genetic Reshuffle 1 - the pathogen's DNA reassembled. Different structure. More work to find a cure
Genetic Reshuffle 2 - a new strain exists. Completely different. Starting from scratch on the cure (Not implemented)
Gastroenteritis - stomach and gut go wrong. They vomit constantly. And it's contagious (Not implemented)
Segmented Genome - the virus split its genetic material into smaller parts. Makes it mutate faster, harder to track (Not implemented)
Horde Instinct - the hordes move with purpose. Cross land, cross water. They're heading somewhere (Not implemented)
Horde Mentality - they stick together. One moves, the rest follow. Pack behavior (Not implemented)
Horde Pheromones - the hordes give off chemicals. Pheromones. Others are drawn to them (Not implemented)
Heat Resistance 1 - it's learning to survive heat. Normal temperatures don't faze it (Not implemented)
Heat Resistance 2 - extreme heat doesn't kill it. Fire, boiling, nothing. It adapts (Not implemented)
Hyper Salivation - something's wrong with their throat. They drool constantly. Saliva everywhere (Not implemented)
Horde Vocalisation - the leaders make distinct sounds. Moans that draw others in. Like a beacon
Hyperosmia - their sense of smell gets way worse. Or better, for them. They can track you by scent
Insect - even insects can get infected now. Not sure how that works biologically (Not implemented)
Insomnia - they can't sleep. Or won't. Exhaustion, fatigue. Still coming for you though (Not implemented)
Lumbrical Hypertrophy - the muscles in their hands get bigger. Once they grab you, good luck breaking free
Liquefactive Necrosis - their organs are half-liquid. Rupture easy. Hit the right spot and they pop
Liquefactive Resistance - their insides don't liquefy as quick. Enzymes get denatured or something. Decomposition slowed (Not implemented)
Masticatory Tension - jaw muscles are way stronger. They bite through thick clothing, leather, everything
Mummification - the badly decayed ones can hibernate. Shut down, wait. Don't assume they're dead (Not implemented)
Naja Mortis - muscles grew around their jaw. They can spit at you from a distance, like some kind of venom (Not implemented)
Gastrointestinal Expansion - stomach and intestines. Vomit and feces are contagious. Disgusting (Not implemented)
Putrefactive Resistance - bacteria can't break them down as fast. Proteins stay intact. They rot slower (Not implemented)
Peptide Surge - something in their blood makes them stronger. Peptides, hormones, I'm not sure. They hit harder
Delirium - irrationality, paranoia. They don't think straight. Makes them unpredictable (Not implemented)
Photophobia - their eyes get sensitive. Sunlight hurts them. At least that gives us something (Not implemented)
Polyphagia - compulsive hunger. They can't stop eating. Or trying to (Not implemented)
Psychosis - the infected have psychotic breaks. Violent, unpredictable. Like something broke in their head (Not implemented)
Regenerative Activation - some of the dead get back up. Nerves regenerate in the brain. Don't assume they're done
Regenerative Bio-Synthesis - even with bad head wounds they can come back. Proteins regenerate the brain. Nothing stays down
Rodent 1 - rats can carry it now. Found infected ones in the sewers (Not implemented)
Rodent 2 - infected rats hunt in packs. They go for the ankles, nasty little things (Not implemented)
Structured Travel - they follow leaders. The horde moves in one direction, faster than they should (Not implemented)
Saliva 1 - their saliva is loaded with it. Salivary glands produce way more than normal
Saliva 2 - nasal mucus too now. Snot, spit, anything from the face. Keep your distance
Temporal Lobe Manipulation - they're drawn to movement. Once you're dead they lose interest. More people turn instead of getting eaten (Not implemented)
Urogenital Expansion - it replicates in kidneys and urinary tract. Bodily fluids, you know (Not implemented)
Vampiric Hunger - they go for the blood, not the flesh. Bite and suck. Victims often turn instead of dying
Water 1 - the virus survives in fresh water. Ponds, rain, humid air. Don't drink untreated
Water 2 - even treated water isn't safe anymore. Chlorine doesn't kill it. Boil everything
Zoonotic Shift - the virus seems to be mutating to infect different species. Heard it makes it harder to predict and contain (Not implemented)
